options.text: A small molecule made from two atoms
A very long chain molecule made from many small repeating units (monomers)

questions.explanation: A polymer is a very large molecule (macromolecule) made by joining many small molecules called monomers together in a long chain.

questions.stem: What type of monomer is needed to form an addition polymer?

options.text: A monomer with two functional groups
A monomer with a C=C double bond (an alkene)

questions.explanation: Addition polymerisation requires monomers with a C=C double bond. The double bonds open up and the monomers join together to form a long chain with only single bonds.

questions.stem: What is poly(ethene) commonly known as?
questions.explanation: Poly(ethene) is commonly known as polythene or polyethylene. It is made from ethene monomers and is one of the most widely used plastics (carrier bags, bottles, packaging).

questions.stem: In addition polymerisation, what happens to the C=C double bond in each monomer?

options.text: One bond of the double bond breaks, and the monomers link together by single bonds
It breaks completely and the monomer falls apart
It stays as a double bond

questions.explanation: During addition polymerisation, one bond of each C=C double bond breaks. The freed bond on each monomer links to the next monomer, forming a long chain connected by single C-C bonds.

questions.stem: Why are many addition polymers difficult to dispose of?

options.text: They are non-biodegradable and persist in the environment for many years
They dissolve in water and contaminate rivers
They are too heavy to transport

questions.explanation: Most addition polymers are non-biodegradable because microorganisms cannot break down the strong C-C bonds in the polymer chain. They persist in landfill for hundreds of years.

questions.stem: What is the monomer used to make poly(chloroethene), also known as PVC?
questions.explanation: PVC (poly(chloroethene)) is made from chloroethene (CH₂=CHCl) monomers. The chlorine atom on each monomer gives PVC its distinctive properties.

questions.stem: How many by-products are formed during addition polymerisation?

options.text: None -- the only product is the polymer

questions.explanation: Addition polymerisation produces no by-products. All the atoms from the monomers end up in the polymer chain, making it highly atom-efficient.
